name: Sticker
basis: why: 'a die-cut sticker is recognised by its edge'; how: white margin grown round the cut, keyline, gloss, peeled corner
note: Uses a subject guess to find the cut line (subject-aware); the flat cartoon colour is not modelled printing.

lumenary.blurb: A die-cut vinyl sticker: the subject in flat cartoon colour, cut out with a thick white border, a soft shadow, a sweep of gloss and one corner starting to peel.

facts.bestOn: One subject on a plain, different-coloured background

why: A die-cut sticker is recognised by its edge. The artwork is cut out along its own outline, a margin of white vinyl is left all round so the cut never touches the ink, and the whole thing sits a hair above the surface. Flat colour and a dark keyline come from the printing. Gloss and a lifting corner come from the plastic.
how: Guess the subject from how unlike the frame’s border each pixel is, and keep the largest patch.
Redraw the picture in flat cartoon colour with ink lines.
Grow the subject’s shape outward and round it off to make the white border.
Add a dark keyline where artwork meets border, and a slanted band of gloss.
Fold one corner back in a mirror line and show its grey underside.
Place it on a coloured surface with a soft shadow.
history: R. Stanton Avery built the first machine for self-adhesive labels in Los Angeles in 1935. Bumper stickers followed in the 1940s. Printed vinyl and computer-driven cutting plotters made custom shapes cheap in the 1980s, and stickers became part of skateboarding and street art. Messaging apps turned them digital around 2011, when large sticker sets joined the emoji.
terms: Cut to the shape of the artwork instead of a rectangle.
A dark outline that holds a printed shape together.
Finding a connected area by spreading from one pixel to all its like neighbours.
paragraphs: There is no trained model here to find the subject, so it is guessed from two cheap clues. The colour of the frame’s border is averaged over a band 4% wide, and every pixel is scored by how unlike that colour it is, plus a little for being near the middle. The score is blurred and cut at a threshold set by the slider. Of the patches that survive, the largest connected one is kept, found by flood fill, and its holes are closed by flooding the outside from the border and keeping whatever the flood could not reach. If the patch is under 5% or over 90% of the frame the guess has failed, and a rounded square is used.

The white border is the shape grown outward. Blurring the shape and taking a low level of the blur does that, and rounds every notch on the way, which is how a cutting plotter treats a sticker too. The artwork is the flat-colour cartoon of the picture, with a dark keyline where it meets the border. The sticker is built on a sheet larger than the picture, so the border has room where the subject runs off the frame. Gloss is a slanted band of light kept to the sticker’s own pixels, and the peel is a true reflection: everything beyond a diagonal line is removed and drawn again mirrored in that line, in grey.

equations.note: How likely a pixel is to be subject: distance of its colour C from the border’s average, and closeness to the centre (u, v from −1 to 1).
The sticker’s outline: the mask M blurred, then blurred again by the border width b, and cut at a low level.
The peel: reflection in the fold line x + y = c.

presets.text: If the cut misses your subject, switch to a round sticker.
A scalloped badge with a wide border looks like a prize seal.
Raise the cut to take in more of the picture.
